prompt: Write a note to a friend about garden tools that never seem to work. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the note only.
final_message:
Dear Harold,

You asked whether I had found a trowel worth owning. I have not; I have found a drawer of them, which is a different thing entirely. Each was bought in the spring with confidence and retired by midsummer, bent at the neck like a defeated clerk.

The hose is the chief offender. It has a nozzle with seven settings, and I have used all seven in the hope that one of them would produce water in a useful shape. Two produce a mist suited to orchids, which I do not grow. One produces a jet that has removed a good deal of mulch and, last Tuesday, my hat. The remaining settings leak at the joint, so that I water my boots with great thoroughness while the zucchini go thirsty.

Then there are the pruning shears, sold to me as "self-sharpening." I do not know who sharpens them, but it is not the shears. They chew a raspberry cane rather than cut it, and the cane, to its credit, bears this with more dignity than I do. I have taken to using the kitchen scissors, and my wife has taken to noticing.

I should say a word for the hoe, which is the single tool I own that does what its name promises; it has never failed me, and for that reason I distrust it a little. A thing that works every time belongs in a better class of household than mine.

The wheelbarrow deserves mention as well. It has one wheel, which is generally considered sufficient, and that wheel has a flat tire that I have patched, inflated, and finally addressed in strong language. It holds air for about the length of a good sandwich. I load it half full as a precaution, so that when it tips (and it will) the disaster is of a modest size, like a minor border dispute and not a war.

I have concluded that garden tools are made for gardens that exist only in the catalogue, where the soil is the color of chocolate cake and nothing is ever rooted under a stone. Mine has stones; it has clay; it has a rhubarb plant that predates the house and resents correction. Against such opposition a trowel does what it can, which is to bend.

Come by on Saturday if you like. Bring your own spade, and do not tell me about it if it works; I could not bear it.

Walter
